image.alt: A tight group of emperor penguin fathers stands on the sea ice with their backs to a snowy wind.

sentences.text: Emperor penguins live in Antarctica, the coldest place on Earth.
In the freezing winter, the father penguins look after the eggs.
Each father holds an egg on his feet, under a warm fold of skin.
The fathers stand close together in a big group called a huddle.
Every penguin is warmed by the bodies pressed around it.
Penguins on the cold outside slowly shuffle inwards, so the birds take turns in the warm middle.
Huddling together, they get through the icy storms of winter.

vocabulary.meaning: a group standing very close together
to move slowly with small steps, without lifting your feet much

questions.prompt: Why do the penguins stand close together?
questions.hint: Look at the sentence after the word huddle. It tells you what the bodies around each penguin do for it.

questions.prompt: Where does a father penguin keep his egg?

choices.text: On his feet, under a fold of skin

questions.hint: Look at the sentence that begins with 'Each father'. It tells you exactly where the egg is held.

questions.prompt: Why do penguins on the outside shuffle inwards?

choices.text: The middle of the huddle is warmer

questions.hint: Read the sentence about the cold outside. Moving inwards gives each bird a turn somewhere warm.

writing.model: Penguins huddle together to keep warm.

image.alt: Fluffy dandelion seeds drift on the wind above a meadow while maple seeds spin down from a tree.

sentences.text: Plants cannot walk, but their seeds can travel to new places.
Moving away helps each seed grow into a plant with its own space and light.
Dandelion seeds have fluffy parachutes that float away on the wind.
Maple seeds have a flat wing that makes them spin as they fall.
Some seeds are hidden inside sweet fruit.
An animal eats the fruit, and the seeds come out later in its droppings, far from the parent plant.
Burdock seeds have tiny hooks that catch on fur and clothes.

vocabulary.meaning: the small part of a plant that can grow into a new plant
air that is moving

questions.prompt: How do dandelion seeds travel?
questions.hint: Find the sentence about dandelions. Their fluffy parachutes are carried by moving air.

questions.prompt: Why is it good for a seed to travel away from its parent plant?

choices.text: The new plant gets its own space and light

questions.hint: Look at the second sentence. It explains what moving away gives the young plant.

questions.prompt: What is this page mostly about?

choices.text: Different ways seeds move to new places

questions.hint: Think about every sentence together. Wind, wings, animals and hooks are all ways of moving seeds.

writing.model: Some seeds float away on the wind.

image.alt: A child stands on grass in the late afternoon sun with a long shadow stretching away from the sun.

sentences.text: A shadow forms when something blocks light.
On a sunny day, your body stops some sunlight, so a dark shape appears on the ground.
As Earth turns, the Sun seems to move across the sky, and your shadow changes.
In the morning, the Sun is low in the sky, so your shadow is long.
Around midday, the Sun is high, so your shadow is short.
In the evening, the Sun is low again, and your shadow grows long.
A shadow always points away from the light.

vocabulary.meaning: a dark shape made when something blocks light
what lets us see, like sunshine

questions.prompt: What makes a shadow?
questions.hint: Look at the very first sentence. It tells you how a shadow forms.

questions.prompt: When is your shadow shortest?
questions.hint: Short shadows happen when the Sun is high in the sky. Find the time of day when the Sun is high.

questions.prompt: You stand with the Sun behind you. Where is your shadow?
questions.hint: Read the last sentence. A shadow points away from the light, so think about which way is away from the Sun.

writing.model: A shadow forms when something blocks light.

image.alt: A child sleeps peacefully in a cosy bed under a blanket, with soft moonlight at the window.

sentences.text: Everyone needs sleep, and children need more sleep than adults do.
Sleep is not wasted time, because your brain and body stay busy.
While you sleep, your brain sorts out what you learned that day and stores it as memories.
Your body also does a lot of its growing and repairing while you sleep.
Without enough sleep, it is harder to pay attention and learn new things.
It is also easier to feel grumpy.
A good night's sleep gets you ready for a new day.

vocabulary.meaning: to rest with your eyes closed, not awake
the part inside your head that thinks and remembers
cross and easily upset

questions.prompt: Who needs more sleep?
questions.hint: Look at the first sentence. It compares children and adults.

questions.prompt: What does your brain do while you sleep?
questions.hint: Find the sentence that begins 'While you sleep'. It says the brain sorts out the day and keeps memories.

questions.prompt: A child stayed up very late. What will be harder for them the next day?
questions.hint: Look at the sentence that begins 'Without enough sleep'. It tells you what becomes harder.

writing.model: Children need more sleep than adults do.

lessons.title: Why We Have Day and Night

image.alt: Earth seen from space, half lit by the Sun shining from one side and half in darkness.

sentences.text: Earth is a giant ball, and it is always spinning.
The Sun can light up only one half of Earth at a time.
On the half facing the Sun, it is daytime.
On the half facing away from the Sun, it is night.
As Earth spins, your home moves out of the dark and into sunlight, and morning comes.
It takes one whole day, 24 hours, for Earth to spin around once.
So when it is daytime for you, it is night on the other side of the world.

vocabulary.meaning: to turn around and around
one of two equal parts

questions.prompt: Why is it night on part of Earth?

choices.text: That half is facing away from the Sun

questions.hint: Find the sentence about night. It tells you which way that half of Earth is facing.

questions.prompt: How long does Earth take to spin around once?
questions.hint: Look for the sentence with a number in it. It tells you how long one spin takes.

questions.prompt: It is daytime in your town. What is it on the other side of the world?
questions.hint: Only one half of Earth gets sunlight at a time. The other side of the world is on the other half.

writing.model: Earth spins, so we have day and night.

image.alt: A big steel ship floats on calm water while a small stone sinks to the bottom below it.

sentences.text: When you put something in water, it pushes some of the water out of the way.
The water pushes back up on it.
If the object is light for its size, that push holds it up, and it will float.
A stone is heavy for its size, so it will sink.
A huge steel ship can float because it is hollow, like a giant bowl full of air.
Its wide shape pushes a lot of water aside, so the water pushes up strongly.
A solid lump of the same steel would sink straight to the bottom.

vocabulary.meaning: to stay on top of the water
to go down under the water

questions.prompt: What does water do when something is put in it?
questions.hint: Look at the second sentence. It tells you which way the water pushes.

questions.prompt: Why does a stone sink?

choices.text: It is heavy for its size

questions.hint: Find the sentence about the stone. It says how heavy the stone is for its size.

questions.prompt: Why can a steel ship float when a lump of steel sinks?

choices.text: Ship steel is a lighter kind of steel
The ship is hollow and full of air

questions.hint: Read the sentences about the ship and the lump. They are the same steel, so look at the ship's shape.

writing.model: Things that are light for their size float.

image.alt: Warm sunlight over a lake, wisps rising into the air, a grey cloud above and rain falling onto hills.

sentences.text: The Sun warms water in seas, lakes and puddles.
Some of the water turns into an invisible gas called water vapour, which rises into the sky.
High up, the air is cold, so the vapour cools into tiny drops of water.
Millions of these tiny drops floating together make a cloud.
Inside the cloud, the drops bump into each other and join to make bigger drops.
When the drops grow too heavy to stay up, they fall as rain.
The rain runs into rivers and back to the sea, and the journey begins again.

vocabulary.meaning: water that has turned into a gas you cannot see
a white or grey shape in the sky made of tiny drops of water

questions.prompt: What is a cloud made of?
questions.hint: Find the sentence with the word cloud in it. It tells you what floats together to make one.

questions.prompt: Why does rain fall out of a cloud?

choices.text: The drops grow too heavy to stay up

questions.hint: Look at the sentence that begins with 'When the drops'. It explains what happens when drops get bigger.

questions.prompt: What is this page mostly about?

choices.text: How to stay dry in a storm
How water rises into the sky and comes back as rain

questions.hint: Think about the whole journey of the water, from the sea up to the sky and back down again.

writing.model: Clouds are made of tiny drops of water.

lessons.title: How an Octopus Uses Its Arms

image.alt: An octopus on a rocky sea floor reaches its eight arms out, suckers gripping a rock and a crab.

sentences.text: An octopus has eight long arms and no bones at all.
Without bones, it can bend its arms in any direction and squeeze through very small gaps.
Each arm is lined with round suckers, and every sucker can grip tightly.
The suckers hold on to rocks and grab crabs and shellfish.
They can also taste whatever they touch.
Most of an octopus's nerve cells are in its arms, not its head.
This lets each arm feel its way and act on its own while the octopus explores.

vocabulary.meaning: a round, soft cup on an octopus arm that sticks to things
to hold on to something tightly

questions.prompt: How can an octopus squeeze through very small gaps?
questions.hint: Look at the first two sentences. They tell you what an octopus does not have.

questions.prompt: What can the suckers do?
questions.hint: Read the sentences about the suckers. One says they hold on, and one says what else they can do.

questions.prompt: How can one arm explore a gap by itself?

choices.text: The arm has lots of nerve cells

questions.hint: Look at the sentence about nerve cells. Then read the last sentence to see what that lets each arm do.

writing.frame: An octopus can squeeze through small gaps because ___

image.alt: A horseshoe magnet pulls steel paper clips toward it, while a gold ring and a drinks can lie untouched nearby.

sentences.text: A magnet can pull some things toward it without touching them.
Magnets attract iron and steel, so a fridge magnet sticks to a steel fridge door.
But magnets do not attract every metal.
Copper, aluminium and gold are metals that a magnet will not pick up.
That is why a magnet will not stick to an aluminium drinks can.
Every magnet has two ends, called poles.
Two different poles pull together, but two matching poles push each other away.

vocabulary.meaning: an object that pulls iron and steel toward it
to pull something closer
a hard, shiny material such as iron, steel or gold

questions.prompt: Which of these would a magnet pick up?
questions.hint: Magnets attract iron and steel. Look at the sentence that lists the metals a magnet will not pick up.

questions.prompt: What happens when two matching poles meet?
questions.hint: Read the last sentence. It tells you what different poles do and what matching poles do.

writing.frame: A fridge magnet sticks to the fridge because ___

image.alt: A map of a small island town spread on a table, with a river, roads and a park seen from above.

sentences.text: A map is a drawing of a place as if you were looking down from high above.
Real places are far too big to draw at their true size.
So mapmakers shrink everything by the same amount, and this is called drawing to scale.
On some maps, one centimetre on the paper stands for one whole kilometre on the ground.
Maps use small marks called symbols, such as blue lines for rivers.
A box called a key tells you what each symbol means.

vocabulary.meaning: a drawing that shows a place from above
how much smaller things on a map are than the real place
a small mark or picture that stands for something

questions.prompt: How does a map show a place?

choices.text: As if you were looking up from the ground
As if you were looking down from above
As if you were standing at the side

questions.hint: Read the first sentence. It tells you where you would be looking from.

questions.prompt: Why do mapmakers shrink everything?

choices.text: Real places are too big to draw at their true size

questions.hint: Look at the second sentence. It explains the problem with drawing real places.

questions.prompt: Where should you look to find out what a symbol means?

choices.text: On the back of the map
In the middle of the map

questions.hint: Read the last sentence. It names the box that explains each symbol.

lessons.title: Why the Moon Seems to Change Shape

image.alt: A row of Moons across a night sky showing a thin crescent, a half Moon and a full Moon.

sentences.text: The Moon does not make its own light.
We see it shine because sunlight bounces off it.
The Sun always lights up one half of the Moon.
As the Moon travels around Earth, we see different amounts of that sunny half.
When the whole sunny half faces us, we see a round full Moon.
When it faces away from us, we can hardly see the Moon at all.
In between, we see a thin crescent, a half Moon and other shapes.
The whole pattern takes just over four weeks, and then it begins again.

vocabulary.meaning: to give out or send back bright light
a thin curved shape, like a slice of the Moon

questions.prompt: Where does moonlight come from?
questions.hint: Look at the first two sentences. The Moon makes no light of its own, so think about where the light comes from.

questions.prompt: Why does the Moon seem to change shape?

choices.text: We see different amounts of its sunny half

questions.hint: Find the sentence that begins 'As the Moon travels'. It explains what changes as the Moon moves.

questions.prompt: Tonight the Moon looks round and full. Which part is facing us?
questions.hint: Read the sentence about a round full Moon. It tells you how much of the sunny half we can see.

image.alt: An old stone arch bridge crosses a river, with a horse and cart on top and the curve meeting the banks.

sentences.text: Every bridge must hold up its own weight and the weight of everything that crosses it.
A simple beam bridge is a flat path resting on supports at each end.
If a beam is too long, it bends and sags in the middle.
An arch bridge has a curved shape instead.
When a heavy load presses down on an arch, the curve passes the weight along to the ground at each end.
Stone arch bridges are so strong that some built by the ancient Romans are still standing.
Some very long bridges hang from strong steel cables held up by tall towers.

vocabulary.meaning: something built so people can cross over a river, road or gap
how heavy something is
a curved shape that bends up and over, like a rainbow

questions.prompt: What can happen to a beam bridge that is too long?

choices.text: It bends and sags in the middle

questions.hint: Find the sentence that begins 'If a beam'. It tells you what a long beam does.

questions.prompt: Where does an arch send the weight of a heavy load?

choices.text: To the ground at each end
Into the middle of the river

questions.hint: Read the sentence about a heavy load pressing on an arch. It says where the curve passes the weight.

questions.prompt: How do we know stone arch bridges can last a very long time?

choices.text: Some built by the ancient Romans are still standing

questions.hint: Look at the sentence about the ancient Romans. The Romans lived a very, very long time ago.

writing.frame: An arch bridge is strong because ___

image.alt: A child rests a hand on their chest after running in a park, with a soft glowing heart shown inside.

sentences.text: Your heart is a strong muscle about the size of your fist.
It sits in your chest, just a little to the left of the middle.
Each time it squeezes, it pushes blood into tubes called blood vessels.
The blood travels all around your body and then comes back to your heart.
On its way, it carries oxygen from your lungs to every part of you.
When you run, your muscles need more oxygen, so your heart beats faster.
You can feel each beat as a pulse in your wrist or neck.

vocabulary.meaning: a part of your body that squeezes to make things move
a gas in the air that every part of your body needs
the beat of your heart that you can feel in your wrist or neck

questions.prompt: What does your heart do each time it squeezes?

choices.text: It pushes blood into blood vessels
It fills your lungs with air

questions.hint: Find the sentence that begins 'Each time it squeezes'. It tells you what the heart pushes.

questions.prompt: Why does your heart beat faster when you run?
questions.hint: Read the sentence that begins 'When you run'. It tells you what your muscles need more of.

questions.prompt: Where can you feel your pulse?
questions.hint: Look at the last sentence. It names two places where you can feel each beat.

writing.frame: My heart beats faster when I run because ___

image.alt: A tree in autumn with yellow, orange and red leaves, a few leaves still green and some falling.

sentences.text: Leaves are green because they are full of a green substance called chlorophyll.
Plants use chlorophyll to catch sunlight and make their own food.
Leaves also hold yellow and orange colours, but in summer the strong green hides them.
In autumn, the days grow shorter and cooler.
Many trees stop making chlorophyll, and the green slowly fades away.
Then the hidden yellow and orange colours can be seen.
Some leaves also make new red colours at this time.
Soon the leaves fall, and the tree rests through the winter.

vocabulary.meaning: the green stuff in leaves that catches sunlight
the season after summer, when many leaves change colour and fall

questions.prompt: What makes leaves green?
questions.hint: Read the first sentence. It names the green substance inside leaves.

questions.prompt: Why do yellow and orange colours appear in autumn?

choices.text: The green fades, so the other colours show

questions.hint: Look at the sentences about autumn. When the green fades away, what can be seen?

questions.prompt: Were the yellow colours in the leaf during summer?

choices.text: Yes, but the green hid them

questions.hint: Read the third sentence. It tells you what the strong green does in summer.

writing.frame: In autumn, leaves turn yellow because ___

image.alt: A glassmaker uses a long pipe to blow a glowing orange blob of hot glass beside a bright furnace.

sentences.text: Glass is made mostly from sand.
Glassmakers mix sand with a few other materials and heat it in a furnace, which is far hotter than a kitchen oven.
The great heat makes the sand mixture melt into a thick, glowing liquid.
While the glass is hot and soft, workers can shape it by blowing, pressing or pouring.
As it cools, it turns hard, and clear glass becomes see-through.
Glass does not rot or rust.
Old glass can be melted and made into new glass again and again.

vocabulary.meaning: a very hot oven used for melting things
to turn from a solid into a liquid by heating
something runny that can be poured

questions.prompt: What is glass mostly made from?
questions.hint: Look at the very first sentence. It names the main thing glass is made from.

questions.prompt: Why can workers shape glass while it is hot?
questions.hint: Find the sentence about blowing, pressing and pouring. It tells you what hot glass is like.

questions.prompt: Why is glass good to recycle?

choices.text: It can be melted and made into new glass again and again

questions.hint: Read the last sentence. It tells you what can happen to old glass.

writing.prompt: Write one sentence about how glass is made.

image.alt: A bolt of lightning flashes from a dark storm cloud to distant hills while a child watches from a window.

sentences.text: Lightning is a giant spark of electricity in a storm.
In a split second, it heats the air around it until the air is hotter than the surface of the Sun.
The hot air spreads out so fast that it makes a loud boom.
That boom is thunder.
Lightning and thunder happen at the same moment, but light travels much faster than sound.
The flash reaches your eyes almost at once, while the sound takes longer to arrive.
Sound travels about one kilometre every three seconds.
So if you count the seconds between the flash and the boom, you can work out how far the storm is.

vocabulary.meaning: a bright flash of electricity in a storm
the loud boom that lightning makes
a tiny, bright flash of electricity or fire

questions.prompt: What makes the sound of thunder?

choices.text: Hot air spreading out very fast

questions.hint: Read the sentences just before 'That boom is thunder.' They tell you what makes the boom.

questions.prompt: Why do we see lightning before we hear thunder?

choices.text: Our ears are slower than our eyes

questions.hint: Look at the sentence that says they happen at the same moment. It also says which travels faster.

questions.prompt: In a storm, the time between the flash and the boom keeps getting longer. What does that tell you?

choices.text: The storm is moving farther away

questions.hint: The sound takes longer to arrive when it has farther to travel. A longer wait means the storm is farther from you.

writing.prompt: Write one sentence about why we hear thunder after we see lightning.

image.alt: A child pulls a heavy suitcase on wheels along a path, next to a heavy box with no wheels.

sentences.text: Try pushing a heavy box across the floor, and you can feel it drag.
The bottom of the box rubs against the floor as it slides.
This rubbing makes a force called friction, which slows things down.
A wheel helps because it does not slide.
Instead, it turns over and over, so it can roll along the ground.
The part of the wheel touching the ground does not rub along it, so there is much less friction.
That is why a heavy suitcase with wheels is easier to pull than one without.
People have used wheels for more than five thousand years.

vocabulary.meaning: the rubbing force that slows things down when they slide
to move along by turning over and over

questions.prompt: What is friction?

choices.text: A rubbing force that slows things down

questions.hint: Find the sentence with the word friction in it. It tells you what this force does.

questions.prompt: Why is a suitcase with wheels easier to pull?

choices.text: The wheels roll instead of sliding, so there is less friction
The wheels push it by themselves

questions.hint: Read the sentences about the wheel. A wheel turns over and over, so less of it rubs on the ground.

writing.prompt: Write one sentence about something that has wheels.

lessons.title: How Camels Live in the Desert

image.alt: A one-humped camel walks across sandy desert dunes under a hot sun, its wide feet pressing into the sand.

sentences.text: Camels are built for life in the desert, where it is hot and dry and water is hard to find.
Many people think a camel's hump is full of water, but it is really a store of fat.
When there is little food, the camel's body can use this fat for energy.
A thirsty camel can drink a huge amount of water very quickly.
Then it can go for days without drinking again.
Its wide, padded feet spread out on soft sand, so they do not sink in.
Long eyelashes and nostrils that close tightly help keep blowing sand out.

vocabulary.meaning: a very dry place where little rain falls
the big round lump on a camel's back
needing a drink

questions.prompt: What is inside a camel's hump?
questions.hint: Read the second sentence carefully. It says what many people think, and then what is really there.

questions.prompt: Why do camels not sink into soft sand?

choices.text: Their wide, padded feet spread out

questions.hint: Find the sentence about the camel's feet. It tells you how their shape helps.

questions.prompt: A thirsty camel finds a pool after days of walking. What will it do?

choices.text: Drink a huge amount very quickly

questions.hint: Look at the sentence about a thirsty camel. It tells you how much and how fast a camel drinks.

writing.prompt: Write one sentence about how a camel is made for the desert.

lessons.title: What Saturn's Rings Are Made Of

image.alt: Saturn with its wide, bright rings, floating among stars in a deep blue night sky.

sentences.text: Saturn is the sixth planet from the Sun, and it has the biggest, brightest rings of any planet.
From far away, the rings look like solid bands.
Up close, they are made of billions of separate pieces of ice and rock.
Some pieces are as tiny as grains of dust, and some are as big as a house.
Every piece travels around Saturn, like a very small moon.
Ice is bright and shiny, so the rings reflect a lot of sunlight.
The rings stretch very wide, but they are amazingly thin.

vocabulary.meaning: water that has frozen hard
to send light back, the way a mirror does

questions.prompt: What are Saturn's rings made of?

choices.text: Billions of pieces of ice and rock

questions.hint: Read the sentence that begins 'Up close'. It tells you what the rings really are.

questions.prompt: Why do Saturn's rings shine so brightly?

choices.text: The ice reflects a lot of sunlight

questions.hint: Find the sentence about ice. It tells you what the shiny ice does with sunlight.

questions.prompt: Why is each piece in the rings like a very small moon?

choices.text: It only comes out at night

questions.hint: A moon travels around a planet. Find the sentence that says what every piece of the rings does.

writing.prompt: Write one thing you learned about Saturn's rings.

lessons.title: How a Compass Shows the Way

image.alt: A walker on a misty hillside holds an open compass, its needle pointing north across the fog.

sentences.text: A compass has a thin needle that is really a tiny magnet.
The needle balances on a point, so it can turn freely.
Deep inside, Earth itself acts like a giant magnet.
Earth's magnetism pulls on the needle, so one end turns to point north.
Once you know where north is, you can work out south, east and west too.
A compass works even in fog or at night, when you cannot see the Sun or the stars.
That is why sailors and explorers have used compasses for hundreds of years.

vocabulary.meaning: a tool with a needle that shows which way is north
the thin pointer inside a compass
the direction a compass needle points to

questions.prompt: What is the needle in a compass?
questions.hint: Read the first sentence. It tells you what the needle really is.

questions.prompt: Why does one end of the needle point north?

choices.text: Earth acts like a giant magnet and pulls on it

questions.hint: Look at the sentences about Earth. Earth acts like a magnet, and a magnet pulls on the needle.

questions.prompt: Why is a compass useful on a foggy night?

choices.text: It works when you cannot see the Sun or stars

questions.hint: Find the sentence about fog. It tells you why a compass still helps when the sky is hidden.

writing.prompt: Write one sentence about how a compass helps people.
